title: A Receptor Built Into the Destroyer

scenes.tts: Botanists looked for the receptor of the plant hormone auxin at the cell surface for decades. Animal biology said a receptor catches the hormone, changes shape, and starts a cascade. But plants with a broken T I R 1 gene respond poorly to auxin. And T I R 1 is an F box protein.
scenes.caption: Botanists looked for the receptor of the plant hormone auxin at the cell surface for decades. Animal biology said a receptor catches the hormone, changes shape, and starts a cascade. But plants with a broken TIR1 gene respond poorly to auxin. And TIR1 is an F-box protein.
scenes.visual: A surface receptor catches auxin and starts a cascade; then a broken TIR1 plant responds poorly; TIR1 appears as a blue F-box protein.
scenes.narration: Botanists looked for the receptor of the plant hormone auxin at the cell surface for decades. Animal biology said a receptor catches the hormone, changes shape, and starts a cascade. But plants with a broken TIR1 gene respond poorly to auxin. And TIR1 is an F-box protein.

scenes.tts: An F box protein is the interchangeable part of an S C F ligase. These proteins were thought to grab targets and sense nothing. Then, in the same issue of Nature, Estelle's laboratory at Indiana University and, independently, Ottoline Leyser and Stefan Kepinski at the University of York reported that T I R 1 binds auxin itself.
scenes.caption: An F-box protein is the interchangeable part of an SCF ligase. These proteins were thought to grab targets and sense nothing. Then, in the same issue of Nature, Estelle's laboratory at Indiana University and, independently, Ottoline Leyser and Stefan Kepinski at the University of York reported that TIR1 binds auxin itself.
scenes.visual: TIR1 on an SCF ligase grips a target and ignores auxin (thought); two lab cards report; auxin binds TIR1.
scenes.narration: An F-box protein is the interchangeable part of an SCF ligase. These proteins were thought to grab targets and sense nothing. Then, in the same issue of Nature, Estelle's laboratory at Indiana University and, independently, Ottoline Leyser and Stefan Kepinski at the University of York reported that TIR1 binds auxin itself.

scenes.tts: Auxin switches on genes, but repressor proteins of the Aux I A A family hold them off. Without auxin, T I R 1 binds one of them poorly. Auxin fits into a pocket at the exact place where the two proteins touch, and the grip tightens. The repressor is ubiquitinated and destroyed, and the genes come on.
scenes.caption: Auxin switches on genes, but repressor proteins of the Aux/IAA family hold them off. Without auxin, TIR1 binds one of them poorly. Auxin fits into a pocket at the exact place where the two proteins touch, and the grip tightens. The repressor is ubiquitinated and destroyed, and the genes come on.
scenes.visual: Repressor holds genes off, sits loosely over TIR1; auxin drops into the pocket, grip closes; ubiquitin tags, repressor destroyed, genes ON.
scenes.narration: Auxin switches on genes, but repressor proteins of the Aux/IAA family hold them off. Without auxin, TIR1 binds one of them poorly. Auxin fits into a pocket at the exact place where the two proteins touch, and the grip tightens. The repressor is ubiquitinated and destroyed, and the genes come on.

scenes.tts: In 2007, Estelle's group, with Ning Zheng, solved the crystal structure. It showed auxin sitting in the joint between the two proteins. The hormone is part of the joint, a molecular glue. So detecting the hormone and carrying out its effect are a single event.
